## Introduction: Deer Observation Data and Methods

This section presents exploratory patterns in white-tailed deer observations across North Carolina from 2010 to 2020.
The dataset contains 2,891 iNaturalist observation records, including observation dates, geographic coordinates, and quality indicators.

We calculated the annual observation data to analyze the temporal trends.
Additionally, to study the spatial distribution, we used spatial connection technology to match the observation coordinates with the boundary polygons of each county in North Carolina, and summarized and visualized the county-level data.
The analysis focuses on recorded observations rather than the actual abundance of deer.

## Research Question
Are white-tailed deer observations more frequent at a close distance to developed areas that border wildland vegetation in North Carolina?

## Intended Audience 
As white-tailed deer populations in North Carolina increase due to few natural predators, and population growth during off-hunting seasons, human-deer conflicts can become more prevalent. This sometimes mean an increase in vehical collisions. Knowing the number of deer and distance they are away from developed areas bordering wildland vegetation can inform the North Carolina Wildlife Resource Commission on region specific harvest strategies. It can also help land owners and land conservation organizations understand where to watch for deer presence in their neighborhoods and on protected lands.

## Figures and Maps

```{r counting observations by year, include=FALSE}
# Count deer observations by year
annual_counts <- as.data.frame(
  table(df_deer_clean$year)
)

# Rename columns
names(annual_counts) <- c("Year", "Observations")

# Convert year and count to numeric
annual_counts$Year <- as.integer(
  as.character(annual_counts$Year)
)

annual_counts$Observations <- as.integer(
  annual_counts$Observations
)

# View the summary table
annual_counts

```

```{r year_slider, echo=FALSE}
sliderInput(
  inputId = "year_range",
  label = "Select Year Range:",
  min = 2010,
  max = 2020,
  value = c(2010, 2020),
  step = 1,
  sep = ""
)
```



```{r interactive_annual_plot, echo=FALSE}
renderPlot({

  annual_filtered <- annual_counts |>
    dplyr::filter(
      Year >= input$year_range[1],
      Year <= input$year_range[2]
    )

  plot(
    annual_filtered$Year,
    annual_filtered$Observations,
    type = "o",
    pch = 16,
    col = "steelblue",
    lwd = 2,
    xlab = "Year",
    ylab = "Number of observations",
    main = "Annual White-tailed Deer Observations in North Carolina",
    xaxt = "n",
    xlim = c(2010, 2020),
    ylim = c(0, max(annual_counts$Observations))
  )

  axis(
    1,
    at = 2010:2020
  )

})
```
Question: How are white-tailed deer observations distributed across North Carolina counties with different development rate?
Observed pattern: In terms of housing units, the deer observations before the development (2010-2015) spread out more than the once from 2020, which gather in 4 clusters in the counties with more housing units. For vegetation cover changes, the pattern is less obvious: deer observations cluster in both regions with high and low destruction.
Units: Number of iNaturalist deer observation records per county.
Limitation: There were fewer data for 2010 to 2015, so we decided to add all these years up and treat the sum as the pre-development deer distribution. Also, the increase in deer observation may not correlated to development itself, but the increase of people visiting the area and thus seeing more deer.

```{r, include = FALSE}

# Convert deer coordinates into spatial points
deer_sf <- st_as_sf(
  df_deer_clean,
  coords = c("longitude", "latitude"),
  crs = 4326,
  remove = FALSE
)

# Match the coordinate system of the county map
deer_sf <- st_transform(deer_sf, st_crs(NC_map))

# Assign each deer observation to a county
deer_county <- st_join(
  deer_sf,
  NC_map[, c("NAME", "GEOID")],
  join = st_within,
  left = TRUE
)


# Preview the results
head(st_drop_geometry(deer_county)[, c("id", "NAME", "GEOID")])
```

```{r plot_function, echo= FALSE}
plot_it <- function(the_parameter, start_year, end_year) {

  # Filter deer observations by year
  deer_filtered <- deer_sf |>
    filter(year >= start_year,
           year <= end_year)

  # Plot selected land use variable
  ggplot() +
    geom_sf(
      data = NC_map,
      aes(fill = .data[[the_parameter]]),
      color = "black",
      linewidth = 0.2
    ) +
    geom_sf(
      data = deer_filtered,
      color = "cyan",
      size = 0.5,
      alpha = 0.5
    ) +
    scale_fill_gradient2(
      low = "darkblue",
      mid = "white",
      high = "red",
      midpoint = 0
    ) +
    labs(
      title = if (the_parameter == "HU_dif") {
        "Housing Development and Deer Observations"
      } else {
        "Vegetation Change and Deer Observations"
      },
      subtitle = paste(start_year, "-", end_year),
      fill = "Change"
    ) +
    theme_bw()
}
```


```{r interactive_map, echo=FALSE}
# Select housing development or vegetation change
selectInput(
  inputId = "the_parameter",
  label = "Select Land Use Variable:",
  choices = c(
    "Housing Development" = "HU_dif",
    "Vegetation Change" = "VEG_dif"
  ),
  selected = "HU_dif"
)

# Select deer observation period
selectInput(
  inputId = "yearPeriod",
  label = "Select Observation Period:",
  choices = c(
    "2010–2015" = "before",
    "2016–2020" = "after"
  ),
  selected = "before"
)

# Display interactive map
renderPlot({

  if (input$yearPeriod == "before") {
    start_year <- 2010
    end_year <- 2015
  } else {
    start_year <- 2016
    end_year <- 2020
  }

  plot_it(
    input$the_parameter,
    start_year,
    end_year
  )

})
```
